The baker's furnace was essential to village life in Goa because bread was an important part of the people's daily food and social customs. Bread was needed at breakfast and on occasions such as marriages, feasts and festivals. The baker supplied loaves and sweet breads to the villagers. His profession had been handed down from generation to generation. Therefore, the furnace represented both food and livelihood. Its presence was closely connected with Goan culture and tradition.

The poet gives humorous clues rather than serious descriptions of wild animals. The lion roars, the Bengal tiger may eat a person, the leopard leaps, the bear hugs, the hyena laughs and the crocodile sheds tears. These exaggerated descriptions make the dangerous animals amusing. The poet also uses rhyme and wordplay to make identification playful. The contrast between danger and humour makes the poem entertaining. Thus, the poet turns identifying wild animals into a funny game.

Anne Gregory's beautiful hair and appearance attract people, but the poem questions whether such attraction is true love. Human beings are often attracted by outward beauty and may not see the inner qualities of a person. Physical beauty is temporary and can change. The poet says that only God can love a person for the self alone. Therefore, genuine love should not depend only on appearance. The poem gives greater importance to inner worth than physical beauty.

Thus education completely changes her life and gives her the courage to take her own decision.

Lencho expected a good harvest because his crop was growing well. Suddenly a severe hailstorm destroyed the entire crop and left him helpless. He wrote to God asking for one hundred pesos to recover from the loss. The postmaster collected money from his employees and friends and sent Lencho seventy pesos. Lencho was happy that God had answered him but became angry because the amount was less than he had requested. He believed that the post-office employees had stolen the remaining money. Thus his expectation, partial fulfilment and disappointment followed one another. OR The pilot began his flight with pleasant feelings because he was returning home and was looking forward to having breakfast with his family. The night was clear and the moon was shining. Soon he saw a huge storm ahead and entered the dark clouds. His compass and radio stopped working, leaving him lost and frightened. A mysterious black aeroplane appeared and guided him through the storm. After landing, he learned that the control centre had seen no other aeroplane. The pleasant flight had therefore turned into a challenging and mysterious experience.

The young seagull was afraid that his wings would not support him. His brothers and sister flew around him and encouraged him, while his parents called to him from the ledge. His parents refused to carry him and made him face his fear himself. Finally, his mother came near him with a piece of fish and then flew away. Driven by hunger, he jumped towards the food and spread his wings. He discovered that he could fly and soon joined his family confidently. OR Buddha taught that human life is temporary and is inseparably connected with suffering. Birth, old age, disease and death are unavoidable facts of life. Kisa Gotami learned this truth when she could not find a single house untouched by death. She understood that death comes to all mortals and that grief cannot bring the dead back. Buddha taught that attachment and desire increase sorrow. Acceptance of the truth of mortality helps a person overcome grief and move towards peace.

A tiger is happier in its natural habitat because it can move freely, hunt prey and live according to its instincts. In the zoo it is confined behind bars in a small cage. It walks angrily along the cage and cannot use its strength freely. At night it hears the patrolling cars instead of the sounds of the jungle. The poem contrasts the tiger's natural freedom with the misery of captivity. Thus the poet shows that wild animals should live freely in their natural surroundings. A new ball cannot replace what he has lost. He must learn to accept loss instead of expecting someone to replace everything for him. The experience is his first important lesson in understanding the nature of loss. It helps him move towards maturity and responsibility.

Google – an online friend: Google can be a useful online friend for students when it is used wisely. It helps us find information, meanings, maps and educational resources quickly. It allows students to explore subjects beyond their textbooks. It can help us understand difficult concepts and prepare projects. However, every website does not provide reliable information. Students should check important information with trusted sources, books and teachers. Excessive use of the internet can waste time and reduce concentration. Safe browsing and protection of personal information are also important. Google should support learning rather than replace books or teachers. A student should search with a clear purpose and avoid distracting content. Educational videos can make difficult topics easier to understand. Online dictionaries can improve vocabulary and pronunciation. Maps and images can also make learning more interesting. At the same time, students should develop the habit of reading printed books. Responsible use of Google makes learning wider and faster. Therefore, Google can truly be an online friend when it is used carefully and intelligently. It can also help students revise quickly. Wise use keeps technology under the student's control. OR Water pollution – A threat to life: Water is essential for human beings, animals and plants. Yet rivers, lakes and groundwater are polluted by sewage, industrial waste, plastic and harmful chemicals. Polluted water spreads diseases and destroys aquatic life. It also makes clean drinking water scarce. We should treat sewage and industrial waste before releasing it into water bodies. Plastic and other waste must never be dumped into rivers and lakes. Farmers should use fertilisers and pesticides carefully. Rainwater harvesting and water conservation can protect valuable resources. Communities should keep local water bodies clean. Schools can teach children about the importance of clean water. Governments must enforce pollution-control laws strictly. Industries should adopt safe waste-management systems. Citizens should reduce plastic use and dispose of waste responsibly. Every person has a role in protecting water. Clean water is necessary for a healthy future. Therefore, preventing water pollution is not only an environmental duty but also a duty towards life itself. Public awareness is essential for lasting improvement. Protecting water is protecting life.
